name: Greenish White
lede: Greenish white is the sixth white in Werner's colour chart, a snow white with a trace of green, shown on a goldcrest's feathers, a narcissus petal and a lump of calc sinter.

sections.title: Werner's sixth white
sections.body:
Greenish white is number 6 among the whites in Werner's colour nomenclature, as Patrick Syme printed it in 1814 and 1821 [1][2]. The recipe beside it describes snow white tinted with a hint of emerald green and ash grey [2]. The three examples are the vent coverts of the golden-crested wren, now called the goldcrest, the polyanthus narcissus and the mineral calc sinter [2].

Syme kept five of Werner's original whites in 1821, this one among them, and added two from his own 1814 edition and one from the system of Lenz [2]. The name also turns up in Baty's comparison charts of the nomenclatures that followed Werner, up to Syme's second edition [3]. Its neighbors in the chart are [[greyish-white]] at number 8 and the plain *snow white* that opens the series [2].

sections.title: Greenish white in the ground
sections.body: Mineral descriptions are where the name started, and it still turns up there. Copperas, the iron sulfate mineral melanterite, is a greenish white that Rutley compared to furnace slag [4]. Phosgenite, a lead chloride carbonate, can be white, grey, brownish yellow, greenish white or pinkish white, depending on its impurities [5]. In mineral description, a tint like this is simply part of how a specimen is recognised [4][5].

sections.title: Whites change with the light
sections.body:
The tint in a white is often borrowed from its surroundings. In his *Science de la peinture*, Vibert wrote that a white wall in full sunlight is never simply white, and he named pinkish, yellowish and greenish whites as the tints it takes from nearby reflections, as Gage quotes him [6]. Livingstone makes the same point with flashlights: under green light a white table still looks white, but a greenish white, while a red tomato looks black because it reflects no green [7].

Pastoureau finds three whites in Rembrandt's *Anatomy Lesson of Doctor Tulp* of 1632: a brilliant white for the neckwear, a dull white for the cloth over the body, and a greenish white for the corpse of the executed man [8]. Hold a sheet of paper beside a green lawn or a wall of leaves and the same effect appears on the paper.

sections.title: On screen it is a cream
sections.body:
The swatch, #F2EBCD, comes from a scan of an aged Werner chart and is approximate [9]. Its a* value is only -2.5, just on the green side of neutral, and ISCC-NBS reads it as yellowish white [9]. The nearest named color is [[ecru]], 4.2 CIEDE2000 units away [9].

On the aged paper, Werner's Snow White, Yellowish White and Orange-coloured White fall within 1.3 units of it, and Snow White is only 0.9 away [9]. The green that gave the color its name cannot be seen on screen, which is why the swatch is better read as a family of old whites than as a green.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch fills at least five per cent of the canvas in 399 works, or 1.7 per cent [10]. It is almost entirely a light: 100 per cent of its area counts as highlight [10]. It is 5.5 times as common in Chinese painting as in the archive as a whole, with 59 of 635 works, and the peak decade is the 1780s, with 18 of 430 paintings [10].

Among painters, [[painter:george-hendrik-breitner|Breitner]] carries it in 5 of his 50 works and [[painter:john-singer-sargent|Sargent]] in 14 of 287 [10]. The picture where it covers most canvas is an eighteenth-century [[painting:aic-142422|Purple Heron]] at 84 per cent, and a Hiroshige II print sketch, [[painting:aic-7688|Sketch for Autumn Moon at Ishiyama Temple]], follows at 77 per cent [10]. All of this is as photographed: aged, varnished paintings and paper, a color match and not a pigment test [10].
